requirements-analysis.summary: Use Claude to draft, critique and stress-test requirements and use cases from real inputs, keeping every requirement traceable to a source and every decision with the stakeholders.
points: Claude adds most value as a critical reader of requirements: ask it to find gaps, ambiguous terms, missing edge cases, conflicting statements and unmeasurable criteria, and to propose testable acceptance criteria.
Give Claude the real inputs (workshop notes, transcripts, the actual process with steps, owners, volumes and pain points). A generic question such as "what should we automate?" gets a generic list.
Ask Claude to separate what stakeholders explicitly said from what it inferred, and to list open questions for the next meeting. Inferred requirements are hypotheses to confirm, not findings.

Insist on traceability: every requirement should cite the input it came from (a survey question, a transcript, a policy). Anything without a source is labelled an assumption that needs an owner, not silently kept.
Vague acceptance criteria ("fast", "promptly", "user-friendly") are a red flag. Supply real targets and ask Claude to rewrite them as measurable statements with thresholds and conditions.

Claude will fill gaps with plausible content: a requirements document may contain features nobody asked for (the invented "SSO section"). Regenerating with a bigger model does not fix this; traceability checks do.

Do not ask Claude to approve requirements as "complete" or "ready", to sign off on the client's behalf, or to estimate the team's story points; those depend on knowledge and accountability Claude does not have.

Use-case analysis works best with explicit criteria: frequency, how rule-based the task is, drafting or summarising load, risk of error, and what data it would need. Ask Claude to score each candidate step against them.
Data policies apply to requirements work too: use anonymised summaries or respondent groups for traceability rather than uploading names, and never fabricate personas as stand-in stakeholders.
Requirements are decisions the organisation owns. Claude drafts and challenges; stakeholders confirm, prioritise and sign off.

docs.title: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations exam guide (Domain 4)

research-planning.summary: Choose the right Claude approach for research, planning and process optimisation: research mode with citations for current external facts, structured process descriptions or measured data for bottleneck analysis, and Projects for plans that are regenerated under stable constraints.
points: Research mode (paid plans) runs multiple linked web searches, can also draw on enabled connectors such as Gmail, Calendar and Drive, and returns a report with citations. Web search must be enabled for it to work, and it uses usage limits faster than ordinary chat.
For current market, pricing or regulatory questions, do not rely on recall from training data: it has a cutoff and no source dates. Use research mode or supply the sources yourself.
Citations are for checking, not a substitute for it. Verify the claims a decision rests on against primary sources (the regulator's text, the vendor's own page).
Scope research prompts: state the jurisdiction, the as-of date and the audience, and ask Claude to flag where sources disagree or are older than a threshold.
Process optimisation starts with a faithful description of the current process: steps, owners, handoffs, volumes and wait times. Claude can then map it, locate queues and propose measurable changes.

Claude analyses the process as described, not as lived. If the documented procedure may be wrong or incomplete, feed Claude measured data (anonymised timestamps, volumes) and compare the two views before acting.
Self-reported confidence and re-asking the same question with the same inputs do not improve an analysis; new evidence does.
Validate proposed changes with the people who do the work, and set up a measurement (before and after) so the effect of the change can be shown.

For plans that repeat under stable constraints (term calendars, campaign plans, rota rules), put the constraints in a Project as knowledge, specify the output format in the instructions, and regenerate in a fresh chat each time inputs change.
Ask for outputs that make review easy: a table with a column showing which rule or constraint each decision satisfies, and an artifact (for example CSV) when the plan must be loaded elsewhere.
Keep publication and external actions human: generating a plan is not the same as writing it into calendars or sending it out. Reviewers decide when it is final.
Other organisations' plans found by research do not contain your internal constraints; internal planning inputs must come from you.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

solution-design.summary: Use Claude as a thinking partner to generate alternatives, critique designs from stakeholder viewpoints and iterate on evidence from pilots, while humans make the design and go/no-go decisions.
points: Ask Claude for two or three alternative designs with trade-offs rather than a single recommendation; compare and choose with the team, then iterate on the chosen design.
Claude tends to affirm a design it is asked to approve. "Is this optimal?" is not a test. Ask for critique instead: risks, failure modes, missing steps, what a sceptical reviewer would say.

Role-based critique is cheap and effective: ask Claude to review the design as a frontline agent, a privacy officer, a finance approver or a customer, to surface objections before real stakeholders raise them.
Pilot on a labelled sample of real (anonymised) inputs, for example 50 items compared against human labels, before scaling. A demo on three hand-picked examples proves nothing.

Iterate by diagnosing: group the failures, find the common cause (an outdated document, a missing category, an ambiguous instruction), change one thing, and rerun the same test set. Do not rewrite the test until it passes.

Instruction pleading ("always answer correctly", "handle regulatory complaints perfectly") does not fix a design defect. Change the design: add a classification and routing step, a human checkpoint, or the missing knowledge.

Place human judgement where errors are costly: fraud indicators, disputed cases, regulatory complaints, legal or financial answers. Automate the low-risk, repetitive part and expand only as measured accuracy justifies it.
Keep the knowledge the process depends on current (for example a returns policy that changes monthly) as part of the design, not as an afterthought.

Escalate to Architects or Developers when the solution genuinely needs an API integration, an agent or custom software; do not escalate a problem that can be solved in Claude.ai with a routing rule and a review step.
Go/no-go, rollout scope and risk acceptance are decisions for the PM and sponsors, informed by pilot data, not delegated to Claude.
Keep a person as the final sender or approver for outbound communications during and after pilots.

docs.title: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations exam guide (Domain 4)
How can I create and manage projects?

workflow-integration.summary: Integrate Claude at the workflow steps where it adds value (classifying, summarising, extracting, drafting) with human checkpoints before consequential or irreversible actions, define handoffs, and measure the effect.
points: Map the existing workflow first, then place Claude at specific steps rather than replacing the process. Typical high-value steps: classify and route, summarise, extract into a checklist, draft a reply or document.

Keep a human checkpoint before external or irreversible actions: sending email to vendors or customers, publishing content, writing to calendars or systems of record, and any legally required decision (for example eligibility decided by a caseworker).

Define ownership and handoffs explicitly: which step Claude produces, in what format, and which steps stay human (fact check, approval, decisions). This is what makes the integration repeatable across a team.
Route consequential topics to people: pay, benefits, contract terms, disputed invoices, fraud indicators, regulatory complaints. Claude handles the first-line and drafting load around them.
Do not remove the independent review step because "Claude checks its own work"; self-review by the same model is not verification.
Do not mandate Claude for every task; integrate where it helps and let measurement guide expansion.

Connectors (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Slack, custom MCP) let Claude read live data and take actions, but by default Claude asks for approval before actions such as sending email. Keep that approval where policy requires human sign-off; on Team and Enterprise plans owners control whether members may switch it off.
Do not engineer around a control (for example building a service-mailbox integration to avoid the approval prompt); that hides the policy violation rather than removing it.
Measure before and after: time per item, revision rounds, error rate, processing time in a pilot with a comparison group. Budget holders and committees fund evidence, not enthusiasm.
Redesign versus augment: even a redesigned workflow keeps verification of extracted details (handwriting, scans), keeps legally required human decisions, and starts with a measured pilot.
Waiting for a perfect system integration forgoes value that a Project with the right documents delivers now; escalate to developers when the technical need is real.

docs.title: Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities

value-communication.summary: Explain Claude's benefits and limits to stakeholders honestly: quantify what was measured, say what was not, describe how the tool actually works, and keep the human role and data rules visible.
points: Pair every benefit with the core limitation: outputs are probabilistic and can contain fluent, confident errors, so facts and decisions need human verification. Say what the verification step is.

Never promise guarantees of accuracy or compliance. No configuration makes Claude "always accurate" or "never off-brand"; use measured results (for example 92% of drafts needed no voice edits) instead of absolutes.

Describe mechanisms correctly: Project knowledge is reference material Claude draws on; Claude is not "trained on" a company's documents and does not become more accurate by being used more. Memory carries context between chats; it is not learning.
Outputs vary between runs; a draft approved once does not certify future drafts. Claude has a training cutoff and does not monitor regulations in real time.
Report pilot results in full: the drafting-time saving and the unchanged review load and the correction rate. Omitting the inconvenient number misleads the decision-maker and costs trust later.

Recommend conclusions the data support (redeploy saved time, extend the pilot) and decline the ones they do not (headcount cuts inferred from one task's time saving, decision quality inferred from speed).

When claims must be evidence-based (procurement, legal review), state what was measured and how, what was not measured, and that decisions remained with staff. Resist both overclaiming and unnecessary silence.
Include data handling in any stakeholder briefing: which data the organisation's policy permits in prompts and knowledge, and how the plan in use handles it.

Claude has no knowledge of the organisation's students, customers or staff beyond what it is given; professional judgement (teachers, caseworkers, compliance staff) remains essential and should be described as such.
Set expectations about escalation: some needs (system integrations, agents, custom software) belong to Architects and Developers, and saying so is part of honest scoping.
Hiding the use of Claude is not required; describing what it does, what people still do, and the evidence is.
